title: Condolences in Spanish: What to Say When Someone Dies
seo_title: Condolences in Spanish: What to Say When Someone Dies
meta_description: Condolences in Spanish: what to say in person, in a card or by message, phrases for funerals, how to offer help and the expressions to use with care.

body_html:
Knowing how to offer condolences in Spanish matters most at the very moment it feels hardest to find words. When someone you know loses a loved one, you don’t need eloquence. You need a few sincere phrases, an understanding of the customs and the courage to show up. This guide gives you what to say in person, what to write in a card or message, and a few expressions to use with care.

Key takeaways
  • Lo siento mucho and Mi más sentido pésame are the two core phrases.
  • Short and sincere is better than long and formal.
  • Offer specific help: ¿Te llevo algo de comer?
  • Avoid phrases that minimize the loss, such as “at least…”.
{{toc}}

The core phrases for condolences in Spanish

SpanishEnglishWhen to use it
Lo siento mucho.I’m so sorry.Always appropriate
Mi más sentido pésame.My deepest condolences.Formal, in person or in writing
Mis condolencias.My condolences.Formal and brief
Te acompaño en el sentimiento.I share your sorrow.Traditional, especially in Spain
Siento mucho tu pérdida.I’m very sorry for your loss.Natural and warm
No tengo palabras.I have no words.Honest when you are shocked

The word pésame comes from me pesa, “it weighs on me”, as the RAE dictionary explains. That image says a lot about what condolences mean: sharing the weight.

What to say in person

At a wake or funeral, people usually approach the family, embrace them and say a short phrase. You don’t need to say more than this:

  • Lo siento muchísimo, María. Aquí estoy para lo que necesites. I’m so sorry, María. I’m here for whatever you need.
  • Tu padre era una persona maravillosa. Your father was a wonderful person.
  • Lo voy a recordar siempre. I will always remember him.
  • Un abrazo muy fuerte. A big hug. (often said while hugging)

Silence and a hand on the shoulder are also a language. You don’t have to fill every pause.

{{image:2}}

Messages and cards

For a card, an email or a message, a slightly fuller structure works well: acknowledge the loss, say something about the person, and offer support.

  • Querida Ana: Lamento profundamente la pérdida de tu madre. Siempre recordaré su generosidad. Estoy contigo en estos momentos tan difíciles. Un abrazo muy fuerte.
  • Estimada familia López: Les envío mi más sentido pésame. Los acompaño en su dolor. (formal, plural)
  • Acabo de enterarme. Lo siento mucho, de verdad. Si necesitas algo, cuenta conmigo. I just found out. I’m truly sorry. If you need anything, count on me. (message)

Offering help

“Let me know if you need anything” is kind, but grieving people rarely ask. Specific offers are easier to accept:

  • ¿Te llevo algo de comer esta semana? Can I bring you some food this week?
  • Puedo recoger a los niños del colegio. I can pick the kids up from school.
  • ¿Quieres que te acompañe? Would you like me to go with you?
  • Te llamo mañana para ver cómo estás. I’ll call you tomorrow to see how you are.

Funeral vocabulary

SpanishEnglish
el velorio / el velatoriothe wake
el funeralthe funeral
el entierrothe burial
la esquela / el obituariothe death notice / obituary
el lutomourning
fallecerto pass away (more gentle than morir)

In many Spanish-speaking countries the wake happens quickly, often within a day of the death, and can last through the night. Families gather, share food and stories, and visitors come and go.

{{image:3}}

Phrases to use with care

  • Está en un lugar mejor. (He’s in a better place.) Comforting to some families, painful to others.
  • Al menos… (At least…) Any sentence that starts this way tends to minimize the loss.
  • Sé cómo te sientes. (I know how you feel.) Better: No puedo imaginar lo que estás pasando. (I can’t imagine what you’re going through.)
  • QEPD (que en paz descanse, rest in peace). Very common in written notices and messages; follow the family’s lead.

Weeks and months later

Grief doesn’t end after the funeral. A message weeks later can mean a great deal: Me acordé de ti hoy. ¿Cómo estás llevando todo? (I thought of you today. How are you coping?). On anniversaries: Hoy pienso mucho en tu mamá. Un abrazo. For more on supporting someone through hard times, see {{link:how-to-comfort-someone-in-spanish|how to comfort someone in Spanish}}.

If you receive condolences

If someone offers you condolences in Spanish, simple replies are best:

  • Gracias, de verdad. Thank you, truly.
  • Gracias por acompañarnos. Thank you for being with us.
  • Gracias por tus palabras, significan mucho. Thank you for your words, they mean a lot.
  • Él te tenía mucho cariño. He was very fond of you.

Nobody expects more than that at a funeral. A nod, a hug and gracias are enough.

Remember too that customs differ between families and regions, from how long a wake lasts to whether people wear black. If you are unsure, a quiet ¿Cómo puedo acompañarlos? (How can I support you?) to a close family member is always appropriate.

Common mistakes

  • Saying lo siento as if apologizing for a small thing. Add mucho or muchísimo and say it slowly.
  • Writing mi más sentido pesame without the accent. It is pésame.
  • Using tú with an elderly widow you barely know. Usted is more respectful.

This is one of the most important situations in my guide to everyday Spanish; for others, from birthdays to congratulations, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

Final thoughts

When someone is grieving, your Spanish does not have to be perfect. Lo siento mucho. Estoy aquí. Said sincerely, those five words are enough, and showing up says the rest.

faq.q: How do you say “my condolences” in Spanish?
faq.a: Mis condolencias or, more warmly and formally, mi más sentido pésame. In everyday speech, lo siento mucho is always appropriate.

faq.q: What does te acompaño en el sentimiento mean?
faq.a: It is a traditional expression of sympathy, especially in Spain, meaning roughly “I share your sorrow”.

faq.q: What should I write in a Spanish sympathy card?
faq.a: Acknowledge the loss, mention something about the person and offer support, for example: Lamento profundamente la pérdida de tu madre. Siempre recordaré su generosidad. Un abrazo muy fuerte.
